data.name: Salammbô: Battle for Carthage
data.detailed_description:
It's the 3rd century BC, despite being supported by thousands of mercenaries, Carthage has just been overrun by its sworn enemy, the Romans, during the first Punic War. In the midst of the killing, Salammbo, the daughter of the commander of the Carthaginian forces, falls in love with the leader of the mercenaries, Matho, who is laying siege to the city as he demands payment for his services.

Inspired by the novel of Gustave Flaubert and the works of Phillippe Druillet, Salammbo: Battle for Carthage puts you in the middle of two of antiquities greatest powers. Can you deliver Salammbo's message before it's too late?

  • Whether crossing gardens full of poisonous fumes or unleashing hell on Mount Solitude, the world of Salammbo is a dark one
  • Get immersed in the 360° panorama of the dark and dangerous world of Salammbo, accompanied by the powerful score from Dvorak's epic "New World Symphony"
  • A series of 3D frescoes forms a unique player's journal summarizing the adventures and providing a new insight into ancient History

reviews.review:
Philippe Druillet is god among men.
Doubly so, seeing how today his phenomenon wouldn’t even be possible as most modern high-skill low-having-anything-to-say artists would probably crucify him as someone who hides his lack of drawing prowess behind elaborate detail.
 
French in all the best ways imaginable, but not in all the worst ways imaginable thanks to the antidote of extreme mortido, it is his body of work that I would point to if asked at the judgement day, whatever was ever the reason for the medium of BD to exist (or whatever you call bandes dessinées in your barbaric Anglophone world).
 
[i]Salammbo[/i] was his magnum opus. You could say, his third magnum opus, after heroic [i]Yragaёl[/i] and hateful [i]La Nuit[/i], but this one he never surpassed in scope.
 
Back in 1860s Flaubert, a supposed realist (in the same way Tolstoy or Dostoyevsky are supposed realists), created an ultraviolent unabashedly romantic tour-de-force to predate and render unnecessary all the future [i]Conans[/i] and the rest of heroic fantasy.
No wonder Druillet turned to it.
 
What of the game though?
 
[b]You’d be best served to consider it [i]Scorn[/i] with more advanced gameplay.[/b]
 
Make no mistake: you’re here for the visuals and the world.
Your main mode of play here is to appreciate Druillet's signature Gothic-Kovil necrobaroque in first person 360° panoramas, in beautiful pre-rendered 3D, and the adventure game mechanics are here mostly to ingrain you into those more than to provide gameplay.
 
Are the mechanics any good?
I wouldn’t know, not really my genre, have little experience in it.
I can only say they’re varied and somewhat interesting.
Sometimes you’re solving [i]Myst[/i]-like puzzles (only much simpler), sometimes you scour available land for objects and points of interest, sometimes you need to pick correct dialogue lines based on common sense, sometimes you apply trial-and-error – say, when trying to adjust a firing trajectory for a siege engine.
It’s never riveting, but also never stale.
 
Here are a few things I found neat gameplay-wise:
1.  A solution to one of the early puzzles comes in handy later in the game.
2.  You have a rudimentary inventory – complete with your character’s doll – and it is employed as a gameplay feature – especially when you’re trying to impersonate someone.
3.  Your world map provides a solution to one of the puzzles.
4.  Knowing the source will help you solve some situations – although it’s not mandatory.
 
Overall, the game’s relationship with the source material (or materials, as Druillet’s [i]Salammbo[/i] is somewhat different from Flaubert’s) is very loose – don’t think you’ve experienced the originals by playing this. Again – you’re here to be in Druillet’s world, first and foremost – the details are secondary.

Spendius, the escapee slave turned mercenary general, is a very appropriate choice of a protagonist, but honestly, it seems like he’s been transformed from a sly crafty and opportunistic adventurer into a Iago-like figure, someone who does ill as an art form – going to heroically great lengths and taking heroically great risks while at it.
 
The [i]Lone Sloane[/i] side of things has been omitted altogether, which is wise. People enter culture shock at the mere sight of local animals, no need to bombard them with brainmelters such as [spoiler]the fact that the Libyan leader is a demigod-like space-faring hero-with-a-thousand-faces who saw the true face of God, and who can wipe populations of entire planets at a handwave, and who doesn’t do that mostly because he’s wading through the universe as if in a dream, opting wholeheartedly into any adventure he encounters – and his current adventure is Hamilcar’s daughter, and to even be here, amongst you mortals, he evaporated his entire ship crew because they tried to persuade him out of it.[/spoiler] [spoiler]No, I don't mean Gaddafi.[/spoiler]
 
But what about all those  negative reviews?
 
Literally half of them is by people who find classical adventure game design inherently disagreeable.
The other half is by people who are outraged that this quarter-of-a-century-old game made by a company that died mid-development, and whose games have consistently received middling reviews by the contemporaries which assured nobody cared for their posterity, is not running perfectly out of the box, and who are genuinely surprised it wasn't slapped out onto Steam as anything other than the haphazard “let whatever little revenue it may generate, trickle”.
 
The first half’s complaints can be ignored, as what are they even doing here?
The second half’s complaints can be ignored, as they sound like pathetic entitled [strike]Flaubert bourgeoisie[/strike] [strike]consumers[/strike] mortals who never heard of dgVoodoo 2.
If you’re lazy like I am, [url=https://steamcommunity.com/app/301670/discussions/0/2146469724202482392/] this thread [/url] has a solution to most of your problems.
 
 
 
A few closing remarks:
 
1. I’ve seen complaints about bugs, but I’ve only encountered two.
One was that an object bugged out (it only happened once).
The other is that sometimes the game boots up running at huge speed (probably because its code is framerate-tied). Just restart till it behaves.
 
2. There are simplistic single-solution battles in the game, and you’ll have to work them either with your common sense or light knowledge of ancient military history ([i]Rome: Total War[/i] experience will do the job too). The battles are fully narrated – both successes and failures – and it’s awesome. I now wish modern [i]Total War[/i] employed AI to do so for their battle replays.
 
3. If there’s a slightest chance that you can play in French, do so.
The voiceover is much better curated and more nuanced.
And the choice of words is overall more poetic than in the Anglophone version.
Don't forget that Druillet himself was involved in the project - and even if he wasn't directing it, his presence at least set the bar in tone which everyone had to strive towards.
Besides, it’ll make puzzles a little more challenging for most of us.
 
It is a particular type of ancient and clearly divine cruel irony that the most exposure Druillet’s work has ever seen came from that MandaloreGaming’s Halloween video mocking [i]The Ring[/i] – which is from the same developers.
 
I never touched that one, but [i]Salammbo[/i] is good at what it does, and don’t let anyone persuade you otherwise.
